Transparent conducting oxides (TCOs) like AZO, GZO, and ITO can exhibit negative real permittivity and smaller optical losses compared to conventional plasmonic metals like gold and silver in the near-infrared (NIR) range.

AZO films deposited by pulsed laser deposition showed a crossover wavelength (where the real permittivity crosses zero) around 1.55 μm, with the properties highly sensitive to deposition and annealing conditions.

For single-interface SPP waveguides, TCOs can provide an order of magnitude better mode confinement than gold or silver in the NIR, but have nearly two orders of magnitude smaller propagation lengths.
The quality factor (propagation length/mode size) of 1D SPP waveguides is about an order of magnitude higher for silver and gold compared to TCOs in the NIR.
TCO-based hyperbolic metamaterials can have a figure-of-merit (FOM) significantly higher than metal/dielectric-based hyperbolic metamaterials in the NIR.
The real refractive index of AZO can reach as low as 0.2 in the NIR, indicating its potential for epsilon-near-zero (ENZ) applications with a non-zero acceptance angle.
Increasing the doping efficiency in AZO to further decrease the crossover wavelength towards 1.55 μm requires optimizing the deposition process, such as using single-target ablation.
TCOs are not as efficient as metals for standard surface plasmon polariton waveguiding applications due to the trade-off between mode confinement and propagation length.
TCOs could have niche applications involving surface plasmons, such as in chemical sensing, where the change in carrier concentration modulates the surface plasmon resonance conditions.
TCOs hold promise for realizing practical metamaterial and transformation optics devices in the NIR and telecommunication wavelengths, where conventional metals perform poorly.
